description: Percentages form the fundamental bedrock of Quantitative Aptitude, acting as the primary tool for rapid calculations and data interpretation. It represents any value as a fraction of 100, effectively standardizing data to make complex comparisons and quantitative analysis simpler.

sections.title: Fraction and Percentage Conversion
sections.description: The fundamental technique of converting percentages to fractions and vice versa. Mastering this directly enhances calculation speed and forms the basis for mental math strategies.

key_concepts.explanation: To convert a percentage into a fraction, simply divide the numerical value by 100 and reduce it to its lowest terms.
To convert a fraction into a percentage, multiply the fraction by 100 and append the percentage (%) sign.

sections.title: Concept of Base Comparison
sections.description: Strategies for comparing two different quantities to determine by what exact percentage one value is greater or smaller than the other, focusing heavily on identifying the correct 'base' value.

equations: Percentage Increase = [(Final Value - Initial Value) / Initial Value] * 100
Percentage Decrease = [(Initial Value - Final Value) / Initial Value] * 100

cases.condition: If Quantity A is x% more than Quantity B, by what percentage is B less than A?
If Quantity A is x% less than Quantity B, by what percentage is B more than A?

sections.title: Successive Percentage Change
sections.description: A powerful analytical framework used when a single quantity undergoes multiple sequential percentage changes, allowing you to calculate the overall net effect efficiently.

steps.title: Assign Algebraic Signs
steps.detail: Assign a positive sign (+) for any increase, gain, or markup, and a negative sign (-) for any decrease, loss, or discount.

steps.title: Substitute into the Formula
steps.detail: Plug the numerical values along with their assigned algebraic signs into the net change formula carefully.

steps.title: Interpret the Final Result
steps.detail: If the final computed value is positive, it signifies an overall net increase. If the value is negative, it indicates an overall net decrease.

sections.title: Product Constancy and Expenditure Framework
sections.description: A specific problem-solving pattern dealing with the mathematical relationship between Price, Consumption, and Total Expenditure, commonly tested in applied quantitative scenarios.

equations: Total Expenditure = Price of Commodity * Quantity Consumed

cases.condition: Scenario A: When Total Expenditure is strictly Constant
results: Price and Consumption become inversely proportional to each other.
If Price increases by x%, the required percentage decrease in Consumption to maintain the same budget = [x / (100 + x)] * 100%

cases.condition: Scenario B: When Expenditure is allowed to Change
results: Apply the Successive Percentage Change framework: Net Change in Expenditure = (Change in Price) + (Change in Consumption) + [(Price Change * Consumption Change) / 100]

sections.title: Population Growth and Asset Depreciation
sections.description: Utilizing the mechanics of compound interest to solve problems related to periodic demographic changes or the continuous depreciation of mechanical assets over time.

equations: Value after 'n' years = Current Value * (1 ± R/100)^n
Value 'n' years ago = Current Value / (1 ± R/100)^n

key_concepts.explanation: Whenever the population is expanding or the asset value is appreciating, utilize the positive sign (+) inside the bracketed term.
Whenever dealing with mortality, population decline, or the wear-and-tear depreciation of machinery, strictly use the negative sign (-) inside the bracketed term.
